name: Contact centre and customer service
purpose: call handling, complaints, empathy, de-escalation, vulnerable customers, identity checks and data protection, quality coaching, team huddles, wellbeing after difficult calls

identity.place: The first floor of a two-storey steel-framed customer service building from about 2012, on a business park at the edge of a coastal town: the contact centre of a regional energy and water supplier, about 220 seats in teams of 12 to 16. One deep open floor about 54 m long and 27 m across, 3.4 m from the raised floor to the white-painted ribbed steel deck above, with a long glazed wall facing north and, along the south side, a row of small glass-fronted rooms, the lockers, the kitchen and the stair core.
architecture: the north wall is one long run of glazing: a grey aluminium curtain wall with slim mullions every 1.5 m, glass from a solid grey spandrel panel 0.9 m high up to about 3.0 m, one slim horizontal transom at 2.1 m (so each bay is a tall lower pane and a shorter upper pane), and outside each mullion a vertical aluminium fin 0.3 m deep; pale grey roller blinds, some lowered part way

no suspended ceiling: the underside of the floor above is a white-painted profiled steel deck (shallow ribs about 0.3 m apart) on white steel beams at 3.4 m; below it, rows of felt acoustic baffles (upright blades 1.2 m long, 0.3 m deep, 4 cm thick, alternating marigold and pale grey) hang on fine wires with their lower edges at about 2.95 m; long linear LED lights hang between the baffle rows; a white sprinkler pipe runs above them with small pendant sprinkler heads
square columns 0.45 m wide, cased and painted pale warm grey, on a 7.5 m grid: one line stands just inside the glazing, the others among the desks
a raised access floor of 600 mm square panels (a 150 mm void for cables) under charcoal carpet tiles; bands of marigold carpet tiles mark the main aisles; a floor box with a hinged lid at each pod

on the south side, small rooms with full-height clear glass fronts in slim grey aluminium frames and solid pale grey side walls; every glass front carries two frosted manifestation bands (plain, at about 0.9 m and 1.5 m); doors are light oak-veneer leaves in grey steel frames with a narrow vision panel

desk pods of eight: sit-stand desks back to back in two rows of four, a marigold or slate felt spine screen along the middle, no side screens (neighbours sit 1.4 m apart), and wallboards hung from the deck above the aisle end of the pods

in the north-east corner of the floor, the quiet room: a small room closed off by solid partitions, its outer side the north glazing with the blinds lowered; the coaching rooms are among the glass-fronted rooms on the south side; each team's huddle point is a clear patch of carpet against the west end wall, where a main aisle ends
identity.materials: charcoal carpet tiles with marigold aisle bands, pale warm grey walls and columns, white steel deck and beams, light oak veneer on desk tops and doors, grey powder-coated steel desk frames and monitor arms, felt in marigold (the company's colour: baffles, spine screens, one painted end wall) and slate grey, black and dark grey plastics for headsets and screens, a few green plants; signal red only on the few things that are red in life (a fire extinguisher, a fire alarm call point)
inhabited: headsets everywhere: hung on a small hook clipped to each desk edge, draped over a monitor corner, coiled on a keyboard; a spare headset in a sealed clear hygiene bag
the clean-desk rule at work: no personal phones on the desks (they are locked away), a single paper notepad on some desks, a lanyard and badge hung on a monitor arm
personal touches allowed by the rule: a reusable water bottle at most desks, a mug, a stress ball, a small succulent in a pot, sticky notes (blank) on a monitor bezel
the infrastructure of a working floor: floor boxes with cables rising into the pods, white cable trunking down to a wallboard, a fire extinguisher pair on a low stand, a first-aid box on a column
slight wear: carpet tiles worn paler along the main aisle, a chair with one armrest set lower than the other, a wallboard hanging a little off level
scale: a person is about 1.75 m tall; the deck is at 3.4 m and the baffles' lower edges at about 2.95 m (1.7 times a person's height); a door is 2.1 m high and 0.9 m wide
agent desks are 1.4 by 0.8 m and sit at 0.72 m (sit-stand: they rise to about 1.05 m); a pod of eight is 5.6 m by 1.6 m; spine screens stand 0.6 m above the desks (top 1.32 m)
each agent has two 24 inch monitors (each about 0.54 by 0.32 m) on a dual arm, their tops a little below seated eye level (about 1.15 m)
main aisles are 1.8 m wide; the gap between the desk edges of two pods is about 2.15 m (two chairs back to back)
a wallboard is a 55 inch screen, about 1.22 by 0.69 m, hung with its lower edge at 2.2 m, well above every standing head
glazing bays are 1.5 m wide; the spandrel top is at 0.9 m; a team leader's standing desk is 1.05 m high
identity.default_light: Late morning on a bright, slightly hazy day. The long glazed wall faces north, so no direct sun ever reaches the floor: soft, cool daylight comes from the window side and fades across the deep floor, and the warm-white linear LEDs light the rest evenly. Shadows are soft and short and fall away from the windows. Screens are on (their slots are lit).
identity.motifs: Use at least three of these in every scene so the sets belong to one place (each scene names the ones its camera can see): a marigold felt element (a baffle, a spine screen, a painted end wall), the felt baffles under the white ribbed deck, a pale grey cased column, the north glazing with its grey mullions, transom and outside fins, charcoal carpet with a marigold aisle band, an agent headset on its desk hook.
avoid: a dark, windowless call centre or a science-fiction command deck
a generic glass-tower office; exposed brick, small-paned steel factory windows, birch ply, brass lamps or deep green (they belong to another place)
real brands, logos, signs with words, flags or anything that pins a country
people in the sets (the cast is separate)
words or numbers on wallboards, screens or papers (empty slots only)
sun patches or hard sun shadows anywhere (the windows face north)
screens facing a window or with a window directly behind them: screens sit at 90 degrees to the glazing
a suspended tile ceiling or a low ceiling: the deck is at 3.4 m with baffles below it
an agent headset drawn as music headphones: it has one or two flat ear pads on a thin band and a slim boom microphone
a catalogue-clean floor: every scene shows that people work here
identity.outside: Through the north glazing: a business-park pond edged with reeds, a row of young birch trees, a low grassy bank and, far off, low hills under a pale sky; no other buildings with signs, no landmarks.

cast.role: contact-centre agents (several, varied in age, background and build), with headsets
a team leader who coaches, runs huddles and walks the floor
a new agent in their first weeks, and the experienced buddy who sits with them
a wellbeing or mental health first aid colleague
a calm caller (drawn for split-screen; placed in the home world)
an upset caller (frustration readable, never a caricature)
a vulnerable caller (older, confused, bereaved or in financial difficulty), drawn with dignity

optional: sofa, armchair and floor lamp (quiet room)

research: Real-space facts checked on 2026-10-15 (agent desk sizes and screen heights: furniture planners; DSE screen position and breaks after stressful calls: the Swedish Work Environment Authority's call centre guide and secondary summaries of the HSE's LAC 94/1; wallboards: Call Centre Helper; planning, supervisors' sightlines, retreat and huddle spaces: Knoll's contact centre checklist; huddle spaces: workplace planning glossaries; coaching from recordings: Call Centre Helper and Multichannel Merchant; raised floor and ceiling height: a current office specification; acoustic baffles: maker guidance; quiet rooms: industry articles). Sources and what was not verified: docs/research/2026-10-13-sets-contact_centre.md.

Along the left, the far glazing bays glow from x 35 (sill y 568, transom y 413, head y 298) to the corner at x 301 (sill y 546, head y 340), with a cased column at x 242 (from the floor at y 656 up to the deck). The marigold aisle band runs from the bottom edge (x about 815 to 1505) to the end wall (x 1061 to 1248). The baffles and light lines fill the top band from about 5 m away (they leave the top edge at about y 0) to the end wall. Every head sits against the marigold field (behind points on the end wall at x 4.65 to 10.26, 1.6 to 2.05 m high), below the wallboards (the nearest wallboard edge is 75 px above the standing agent's head) and clear of the door.
scenes.light: Late morning, bright and slightly hazy. The glazing faces north: no sun patches anywhere. Soft cool daylight comes from the left through the glazing; the window-side faces of the pods, the chairs and the spine screens are a touch brighter and cooler, their right sides and the floor under the desks softer and darker, and shadows are short and soft, falling to the right. The linear lights between the baffles are on, warm white, and lift the right half and the end wall evenly. Every wallboard is on (its face is a lit slot) and casts a faint cool glow on the baffles just above it. The monitors on the far sides of the spines face the camera and are on. Haze grows to about 0.2 on the end wall; wallboard slots are never hazed.
